name: Carla Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy wine, beer and spirits for Harbour Merchants, a drinks distributor serving bars, restaurants and shops along the coast. I use an AI assistant every morning to forecast demand, so I know before the heatwave that we'll need more rosé and lager. Then I spend my day on tastings with producers, price negotiations and juggling shipments. It's thirty years of work and I still enjoy the tastings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the variety and the people: winemakers, bar owners, the drivers. What wears me out is the pace around holidays and the fact that I'm paid less than the new category managers, even though I trained half of them. My partner Dev runs a small bike repair shop, so our income wobbles from month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably about right. The tools I use daily help but they haven't replaced anyone I know. I'd say it to the bar owners who keep asking me if AI will do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not scared of the AI, but I'm nervous about money. Dev's shop earns nothing in January and February, and we've got less than three weeks of savings. If the firm's sales slump, I'm the expensive buyer in a small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the forecasting tool and try to make it better, maybe by feeding it local event calendars. I'd ask for a pay review, using the cost savings from the forecasts. And I'd put 100 a month into a separate account for the lean months of Dev's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I like my work but I know how fragile the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you trusted the tool over a trend. What did your gut say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once saved the firm from a 15,000 overstock of a prosecco that went out of fashion, and I never got credit. The tool flagged the trend and I trusted it. I got a nod in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being paid for what you contribute look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm doesn't know what it has. I'm not blaming anyone. I'd just like to be paid for what I contribute, and I don't want a country where people over 55 get written off.

say: I'd say the tools I use help but haven't **replaced** anyone I know.
I'd say I want to be **paid** for what I contribute and not be written off after 55.
think: I'm not scared of AI but I'm **nervous about money**: Dev's shop earns nothing in January and February.
I'm the expensive buyer in a small team if sales slump.
do: Improve the **forecasting tool** by feeding it local event calendars.
Ask for a **pay review**, using the savings from my forecasts.
Put **100 a month** aside for the lean months.
feel: A bit **uneasy**: I like my work but know how fragile the money is.
S0.quote: I once saved the firm from a 15,000 overstock of a prosecco that went out of fashion, and I never got credit.
fieldNote: Her job looks fairly safe now, but a **self-employed** partner's seasonal income and a thin cushion keep her uneasy.
**Already** uses AI daily and treats it as an ally.
Feels **under-credited** and underpaid compared with younger managers.

steps.text: Feed local event calendars into the forecasting tool
Ask for a pay review using last year's forecast savings
Put 100 a month aside for Dev's lean winter months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what I'm already living. The tool does a lot of the buying logic, and the juniors can run it. I'd tell colleagues to learn it or become the person who fixes what it gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buyer team goes from three to one or two in three years. I'm the most experienced but I'm also the most expensive. The firm might decide the juniors plus the tool are cheaper. That is a rational choice and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward what the tool can't do: tastings, producer relationships and negotiating allocations of rare bottles. I'd sign up for the wine and spirits qualification, which is 900 over a year, and pay from savings. I'd propose a new role to my boss, Helena: head of producer relations. And I'd keep Dev's shop in mind as a fallback, helping with his books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. Slightly sick, but focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Portuguese producer. What exactly made them choose you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A week ago a small Portuguese producer chose to sell to us over a bigger distributor because I'd visited the vineyard. The tool had never been there. That's the thing the AI can't copy, yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does head of producer relations involve that the tool can't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pay system is the problem. Companies pay for tasks, not for trust built over decades. But it's the market. I'd rather adapt than complain, though I'd quietly vote for anything that helps people retrain.

say: I'd say this is what I'm already living: juniors can run the tool, so learn it or **fix its errors**.
I'd say companies pay for tasks, not for **trust** built over decades.
think: I think the buyer team shrinks from three to **one or two** in three years.
I'm the most experienced and the most **expensive**, which is a rational reason to cut me.
do: Sign up for the **900** wine and spirits qualification and pay from savings.
Propose a **producer relations** role to my boss Helena.
Keep helping with Dev's bike shop **books** as a fallback.
S1.quote: A small Portuguese producer chose to sell to us over a bigger distributor because I'd visited the vineyard. The tool had never been there.
fieldNote: Sees her high pay as the target but acts on it, which keeps her **anxious** rather than alarmed.
Bets on human **relationships** with producers that software lacks.
Accepts the market logic but quietly wants **retraining** support.

steps.text: Enrol in the 900 wine and spirits qualification
Pitch a head of producer relations role to Helena
Visit two more vineyards this autumn to deepen ties
Keep doing the books for Dev's bike shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and I wouldn't pretend to understand all of it. I'd be honest at work: we all need a plan. I'd tell people that using the tools well gives us a little time, but not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my desk role is gone by 2029. If the machine can do my job better and cheaper, a company will pick the machine. What's left for me is the human side, but there might be one job for it and fifty of us want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every non-essential cost right away, which gives us about 400 a month. I'd go hard on the producer role, and I'd also ask Helena if the firm will fund me to run the AI system, since I know it well. I'd look at hands-on options like managing the warehouse, because robots are three years behind. And I'd ask Dev if we can sell some bikes and parts online to bring in more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not helpless. I'm the sort who makes lists when I'm frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the budget on the fridge. What would be the first line you'd cross out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev and I sat down and wrote our monthly budget. It's 3,800 in and 3,500 out. If my 2,600 goes, we're in trouble inside two months. That table is on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help if the government acted now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the speed. It's not that change is bad. It's that we're told to adapt in two years, with no savings and no help. Companies and governments could have prepared and didn't.

say: I'd tell colleagues we all need a **plan**, because the tools buy only a little time.
I'd say we're told to adapt in **two years** with no savings or help.
think: I think my desk role is gone by **2029** if a machine does it cheaper.
The human side might leave **one job** that fifty of us want.
do: Cut every non-essential cost to free about **400 a month**.
Ask Helena to fund me to **run the AI system**.
Consider **warehouse** management, since robots come about 3 years later.
feel: **Alarmed** but not helpless: I make lists when I'm frightened.
S2.quote: Dev and I sat down and wrote our monthly budget. It's 3,800 in and 3,500 out. If my 2,600 goes, we're in trouble inside two months.
fieldNote: Her pay of 2,600 is half the **household's** cover, so losing it means trouble in two months.
Reacts with lists and plans; looks for a role **running** the AI.
Blames speed and lack of **preparation** by firms and governments.

steps.text: Cut the household budget by 400 a month
Ask Helena to fund me to run the buying system
Apply for the warehouse manager track
Help Dev sell bike parts online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a useful gap. I'd say to my team that nobody should wait, because the gap is only useful if you use it. I'd probably say it's the scenario where hard work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when it hits. I think I could pivot to producer relations or a consultant role by then. I'd have a few years of reduced income, but I'd probably make it to a small pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, the qualification, in year one. Second, a side venture: tasting events for small shops, maybe 20 a year at 300 each. Third, I'd save 300 a month, which means cutting dinners out. I'd also get my boss to give me the producer role on trial. And I'd keep learning the newest tools, because they change every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a bit of tension. I like the idea of reinventing myself at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the tasting events. Who would pay for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dev about maybe moving to a smaller flat to save on rent. He's not keen, but if it saves 400 a month, we'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your checkpoint in year three look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pivot doesn't work I'd rather know early. I'd set a checkpoint in year three: if I don't have 50 percent of my income from new things, I'd look for a job elsewhere.

I'd say hard work still **pays** in this version.
think: At 63 I could pivot to producer relations or **consulting** and still reach a small pension.
I'd have a few years of **reduced income**.
do: Run about **20 tasting events** a year at 300 each for small shops.
Save **300 a month** by cutting dinners out.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a bit of tension: reinventing myself at 60 appeals.
S3.quote: I'd set a checkpoint in year three: if I don't have 50 percent of my income from new things, I'd look for a job elsewhere.
fieldNote: Five years plus her **adaptability** make her feel in control, and she sets a clear checkpoint.
Side venture and move to a smaller flat show she'll trade comfort for **security**.
Still uneasy since the plan **depends** on the firm and her thin cushion.

steps.text: Finish the wine and spirits qualification within the year
Run 20 paid tasting events a year for small shops
Save 300 a month by cutting dinners out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years: I'd say I feel fine. I'd tell my younger colleagues to get a skill that blends people and tools. For myself, I'd be 68 and almost certainly retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the first scenario where I could reach retirement without drama. Money's still tight, but a decade gives me time to fix it. It's the young ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and pass on my knowledge to Santiago, our junior buyer, as a mentor. I'd save 250 a month and aim to clear our credit card. I'd also set up a small tasting business on the side, since I'd enjoy it into my sixties. And I'd help Dev sell the shop in a few years when he's ready to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually calm, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mentor Santiago. What would you teach him that the tool can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thin savings are what I'd watch. A decade is only enough if we use it. I'd make a rule: no big purchases until the card is cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from a pension system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what would help is a flat, stable pension and decent funding for retraining. If those exist, I'd feel fine for myself and for the juniors.

I'd say stable pensions and retraining funding are what **help**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, 2,600 a month that holds the household up, and nothing in the bank. What would help is a retraining fund that works, a pension I can count on, and my firm telling me honestly where I stand. And, honestly, a little luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I use the tools every day and I'm still the one with the biggest salary on a shrinking team.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I use the tools every day and I'm still the one with the biggest salary on a shrinking team.
portrait: **Carla Costa**, 58, buys wine and spirits for a coastal distributor and uses AI forecasting tools every day.
She is **centre** and adaptive: pragmatic, quick to learn, and quietly sure the market will not reward loyalty.
Thin savings and a partner with seasonal income keep her **uneasy**, and anxious or alarmed when buyer jobs look at risk.
She bets on **producer relationships**, a wine qualification and tasting events as her way to stay useful.
She sets checkpoints and budgets, and would trade a bigger flat for security.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because her 2,600 a month holds the household up and nothing is saved.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining fund that works, a reliable **pension** and honest talk from her firm.
A little **luck**, in her own words.
